clue.text: Earliest piece of rock-music

parts.note: the first music a baby hears is sung while its crib is rocked, not the electric-guitar genre

explanation.surface: A pop historian names the first ever rock record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock-music' suggests guitars and drums; read it as music for rocking a baby, the earliest tune anyone hears.
explanation.definitionFit: A lullaby sung over a rocking crib is the first music in a person's life.

clue.text: "Tricky trial ends in nothing"' (Venetian news-source)

indicators.note: ends in places the next piece at the end of the rearranged word
something tricky is awkward to handle, so the letters are twisted round

parts.note: O looks like a zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A Venetian newspaper headline reports that a difficult court case came to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky' rearranges TRIAL into RIALT. In The Merchant of Venice Shylock asks "What news on the Rialto?", making the Venetian bridge-and-market district a news source.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Venetians gather gossip at this bridge and market district, asking what news is there.

clue.text: Joys of the Camptown illuminations?

parts.note: the song Camptown Races uses the dialect form de for the
lights are illuminations

explanation.surface: A visitor delights in the light displays of a small American town.
explanation.walkthrough: Camptown Races is an old minstrel song ('De Camptown ladies sing dis song'), so its 'the' is DE.
explanation.definitionFit: Joys and pleasures are delights, plural noun for plural noun.

clue.text: They detest a siesta, sang Coward

definitions.text: They detest a siesta, sang Coward

parts.words: They detest a siesta, sang Coward
parts.note: Noel Coward's song about mad dogs in the midday sun says the people of one nation scorn an afternoon nap

explanation.surface: A cowardly person sang about people who hate afternoon naps.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel Coward was an English playwright and songwriter; 'Coward' looks like a timid singer. His song Mad Dogs and Englishmen includes the line about detesting a siesta.
explanation.definitionFit: Coward's lyric names natives of England as the ones who go out in the midday sun and scorn napping.

clue.text: Run on longer than anybody else

definitions.text: Run on longer than anybody else

parts.words: Run on longer than anybody else
parts.note: to keep chattering past everyone else, beating them at conversation, not running a race

explanation.surface: An athlete keeps running after every rival has stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run on' suggests running further; it means to go on talking.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep speaking longer or more forcefully than others is to beat them at conversation.

clue.text: Midnight witchcraft in desert

indicators.note: Mid takes the centre letter of the word that follows it

parts.note: obi, or obeah, is a form of West Indian witchcraft

explanation.surface: Sorcery is practised at midnight in the wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Midnight' splits into 'Mid' (centre of) and 'night', whose middle letter is G.
explanation.definitionFit: A vast arid region of Mongolia and northern China, one of the world's great deserts.

clue.text: First lady in regal shift means to make a purchase

indicators.note: in puts the first lady inside the rearranged letters
a shift moves things about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Eve was the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: A president's wife goes shopping in a fine dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shift' rearranges REGAL into L... RAGE, and 'in' puts EVE inside to make L-EVE-RAGE. 'Purchase' here means a grip or hold, not buying.
explanation.definitionFit: Purchase can mean mechanical grip; leverage is the force or hold that gives such grip.

clue.text: Injunction to overzealous draughtsman in plaintive manner?

definitions.meaning: an instruction to a designer working too hard: draw your designs softly
mournfully, with a sad resonant sound

explanation.surface: A designer who over-presses the pencil is told off in a whining tone.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as PLAN GENTLY, an order to a too-vigorous draughtsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Plangent describes a loud mournful sound, so the adverb means mournfully.

clue.text: Gold trade test

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
a deal is a trade or bargain

explanation.definitionFit: A severe trial or testing experience is an ordeal; medieval trial by ordeal was literally a test of guilt.

clue.text: Georgia's delicate Victorian brilliance

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia, with the possessive S added
light means delicate, not heavy

explanation.surface: Someone praises a Georgian's delicate radiance in the Victorian style.
explanation.definitionFit: Streets and homes of the Victorian era were lit by burning coal gas, its typical illumination.

clue.text: Hire-tent collapsed? How unlucky!

indicators.note: a tent that has collapsed has fallen into a heap, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rented marquee falls down, and someone groans at the bad luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collapsed' rearranges the letters of HIRE-TENT.
explanation.definitionFit: The number superstitiously held to bring bad luck, so its mention suggests misfortune.

clue.text: Tipping part of blast-furnace rubbish '

definitions.meaning: the sloping lower section of a blast furnace, tipping inward, bears this technical name
rubbish in the sense of nonsense, as in an exclamation of disbelief

explanation.surface: Debris from a sloping section of an iron furnace is dumped as waste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tipping' sounds like dumping rubbish, but it describes the slope of that furnace part.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a furnace term for the tapering zone above the hearth and an informal word for nonsense.

clue.text: Money tight for Shaw's captain

parts.note: brass is British slang for money
bound means tied tight

explanation.surface: A captain in a Shaw play is short of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: George Bernard Shaw wrote the play Captain Brassbound's Conversion.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Shaw's play Captain Brassbound's Conversion bears this surname.

clue.text: .Arms talks I evaluate, being ready to jump

parts.note: SALT were the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks between the US and USSR
to grade is to evaluate or rank

explanation.surface: A diplomat assesses disarmament negotiations, poised to leap at an opportunity.
explanation.definitionFit: A zoological adjective for creatures, such as jumping spiders, that move by leaping.

clue.text: Knowledgeable about rays, for example. I cannot drink

parts.note: someone into a subject is keen on and well informed about it
X as in X-rays
I can't is I cannot shortened

explanation.surface: A physicist who knows about radiation declines an alcoholic drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drink' as a noun: an alcoholic one intoxicates. The clue's 'I' was read as the figure 1 in the source text.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcohol is the commonest substance that intoxicates, so an intoxicant is a strong beverage.

clue.text: Article we divers find daunting

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
divers is an old word meaning several or various, so some

explanation.surface: Scuba divers admit they find something intimidating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divers' is not people who dive but the archaic adjective meaning various or sundry.
explanation.definitionFit: Something awesome inspires awe and dread, so it is intimidating.

clue.text: England's opening pair playing and making Bill work

parts.note: the first two letters of the word England
acting is playing a role

explanation.surface: England's opening batsmen are at the crease as Parliament passes a bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening pair' evokes cricket's opening batsmen; here it is the first two letters of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Enacting a parliamentary bill turns it into law, putting it into effect.

clue.text: Disciple in rags?

parts.note: a learner taking part in the charity stunts of a university rag week, not a ragged follower

explanation.surface: A follower of some teacher goes about in tattered clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: A rag is a British university charity event week of stunts, run by undergraduates; 'rags' suggests torn clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A disciple is a pupil, and pupils at university hold rags, so a learner fits both.

clue.text: Tum bared, prepared for a tattoo

indicators.note: the letters are made ready in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A man bares his belly, ready to get some skin art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepared' rearranges TUM BARED. 'Tattoo' is a rhythmic drumming, not skin art.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattoo is a military drum signal or rhythmic beating, so a sustained rhythm of drumming.

clue.text: Cheat greedy people out of 500 pounds

indicators.note: out of puts the greedy people outside the following letters

parts.note: swine are greedy people
D is the Roman numeral for 500
L is the abbreviation for pounds, from libra

explanation.surface: Grasping folk are swindled of a large sum of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' places SWINE around DL, making SWIN-DL-E.
explanation.definitionFit: To swindle someone is to defraud or trick them out of money.

clue.text: Malleable pigment of the post-impressionists?

parts.note: those who stamp impressions on post use a soft coloured substance, not the painters Van Gogh and Gauguin

explanation.surface: An art historian asks what soft paint the post-impressionist painters used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'post-impressionists' points to Cezanne and co; split it as people making impressions (seals) on post (letters).
explanation.definitionFit: The soft coloured wax melted onto envelopes and stamped with a seal makes an impression on mail.

clue.text: Plain nasty

definitions.meaning: plain as in unattractive in looks
nasty as in threatening or unpleasant, of a situation or mood

explanation.definitionFit: Unattractive in appearance, and also unpleasant or menacing, as an angry crowd turning so.

clue.text: Vessel incorporating a form of ancient writing

indicators.note: incorporating means holding something within, so the vessel takes in the letter A

parts.note: a liner is an ocean-going ship

explanation.surface: A ship's cargo includes an old style of script.
explanation.walkthrough: Linear A and Linear B are ancient Cretan scripts, so the clue's 'a' points to Linear A too.
explanation.definitionFit: Linear A and B are scripts of Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece, named by this word.

clue.text: Piece of pot showing writing and funny cartoons

indicators.note: funny suggests something odd or strange, so these letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: An archaeologist finds a potsherd with writing and comic drawings on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'funny' rearranges the letters of CARTOONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient Greeks scratched notes and votes on broken pottery fragments called by this name.

clue.text: Copper on ship is an annoying fellow

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: A police officer on board a vessel is a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman; here it is the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuss is an informal word for an awkward or irritating person.

clue.text: As far as one can go by — direct inner Circle Line

definitions.text: As far as one can go by — direct inner Circle Line

parts.words: As far as one can go by — direct inner Circle Line
parts.note: the longest straight chord across a round figure passing through its centre, not a London Underground route

explanation.surface: A Tube traveller wonders how far the inner Circle Line will take them directly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Circle Line is a London Underground route; here it is a straight line inside a circle, the longest one possible.
explanation.definitionFit: The straight line through a circle's centre is the longest chord, going as far across as possible.

clue.text: Some malignant escorts seen in this French port!

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Sinister companions are spotted in a French harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: A city and port on the Loire in western France.

clue.text: Published numbers making up the crowd

definitions.meaning: issues of a long-running British weekly magazine, each one a copy of it
the crowd as in the people watching a match or show

explanation.surface: Printed figures show how many people made up the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spectator is a British weekly political magazine; its numbers (issues) take its name in the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Onlookers at an event, and copies of a weekly periodical, share the plural name.
